clue.text: European bridge — one leading to a road

blocks.note: a span is a bridge, or the stretch a bridge covers
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
RD is the standard abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: A bridge somewhere in Europe, with one carriageway feeding onto a road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European bridge' reads as one phrase, but 'European' alone is the definition and 'bridge' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Spain is one particular kind of European, so this is definition by example.

clue.text: Inspectors finally have the power to examine closely

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the very end of a word, so only its closing letter is used

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
to be able to do something is to have the power to do it

explanation.surface: Inspectors at last get the authority to look into something properly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests official powers of investigation; in fact 'have the power to' is just the verb CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: To scan text or a scene is to look it over carefully, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: Fruit and a grain

blocks.note: taken as written
corn is a cereal grain

explanation.surface: A shopping list for a healthy breakfast: some fruit and a cereal.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a list of foods, but 'a grain' is simply A plus CORN, while 'Fruit' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically the nut of an oak tree is its fruit, the seed-bearing part the tree produces.

clue.text: Misguided main intent of light-hearted news shows, for example

indicators.note: something misguided has gone astray from its proper course, so the letters wander out of order

blocks.note: twelve letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic complains that the chief aim of jokey news programmes is wrong-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder runs across three small words, including 'of', which looks like it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Television mixing information with entertainment is the blend this word describes; jokey news programmes are a typical case.

clue.text: Runner finally running relay remarkably well

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the very end of a word, so only its closing letter is used
running can mean being operated or processed, so the letters are set in motion and rearranged

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An athlete on the final leg runs a relay exceptionally well.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition uses an old sense: RARELY once meant 'finely, splendidly', not just 'seldom'.
explanation.definitionFit: In older or literary English this adverb meant exceptionally or splendidly, from rare in the sense of fine or excellent.

clue.text: A university somewhere in South America

blocks.note: 'a' as in 'twice a day' means per
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A college located somewhere on the South American continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' looks like a mere article, but it means PER, as in 'ten pounds a head'.
explanation.definitionFit: The country is one of the nations of that continent, so a vague location phrase covers it by example.

clue.text: Educated leader from Estonia impolite about Italy

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the word is taken
'about' means around, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: the opening letter of the country
rude means impolite
IT is the international code for Italy

explanation.surface: An educated Estonian leader is discourteous on the subject of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader from Estonia' sounds like a head of state; it only means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone erudite has great learning, so the word is a close adjective synonym for well educated.

clue.text: Measure developed to protect new log-in information

indicators.note: something developed has been worked into a different shape, so the letters are reshaped
to protect something is to surround and shield it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A security measure is built to safeguard fresh login details.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' looks like a security measure, but it is just seven letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: When signing in to a computer system you type an identifying name alongside a password, so it is part of the login details.

clue.text: True haters awfully bored by a French game

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out in a mess
to be bored by something is to have a hole drilled through you, so another piece sits inside

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
un is French for 'a'

explanation.surface: Genuine haters are terribly bored by some French game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored' reads as uninterested, but it means drilled into: the French article goes inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunt for hidden prizes following clues is a classic party pastime for children, so it is an example of a game.

clue.text: A dessert turned cold

indicators.note: something turned is faced the other way, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
a fool is a British pudding of puréed fruit folded into cream

explanation.surface: A pudding has been left out and gone cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' suggests milk going off; here it flips the pudding's letters. A fool is a British dessert of fruit and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A distant, unfriendly manner is described as cold or standoffish, the figurative sense of the adjective.

clue.text: After extremely routine, heavy defeat, we ultimately change direction

indicators.note: 'extremely' points to the extremes of a word, its two ends, so only those letters are kept
'ultimately' means at the end, so only the closing letter is used

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
a rout is a crushing defeat
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: After a routine thrashing, a team decides at last to change tack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' tells you the defeat comes after the edges of 'routine'; the comma hides that 'heavy defeat' is one unit.
explanation.definitionFit: To reroute is to send something along a different path, so it is a verb synonym for changing its course.

clue.text: Art exhibit everybody enters in Euston?

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: taken as written
all means everybody
Euston is a London railway terminus; the question mark flags it as an example

explanation.surface: An art exhibit that every traveller passes through at a busy London station.
explanation.walkthrough: Euston is a major railway station in London, so 'Euston?' stands for STATION by example; 'in' is taken literally and placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: A large artwork assembled in a gallery space, often walk-through, is called this; it is one type of exhibit.

clue.text: Vivacious friend taken in by an idea only half-formed

indicators.note: to be taken in is to be received inside, so one piece is held within another
something only half-formed is missing its back half, so part of the word is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
the first half of the word
a mate is a friend

explanation.surface: A lively pal is fooled by a plan that was never properly thought through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' suggests being fooled; here it means held inside the first half of 'idea'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vivacious person is lively and full of spirit, which is the everyday adjective sense of the answer.

clue.text: Mythical creature that is alongside headland

indicators.note: alongside means placed next to, so two pieces simply sit side by side

blocks.note: a ness is a headland or promontory, common in British place names
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: A legendary beast is spotted beside a coastal promontory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' looks like a relative clause, but it is the abbreviation i.e.
explanation.definitionFit: The fabled monster said to live in Loch Ness in Scotland is a legendary beast that has never been proven to exist.

clue.text: Weapon raised incorrectly over marine’s head

indicators.note: done incorrectly means put together wrongly, so the letters are in the wrong order
the head is the top or front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A gun was wrongly lifted above a marine's head.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so the rearranged letters sit on top of the M.
explanation.definitionFit: A pistol or similar arm carried at the belt is called this, so it is one kind of weapon.

clue.text: Take advantage of being housed in silent public institution

indicators.note: to be housed in somewhere is to live inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: to keep mum is to stay silent
to use someone is to take advantage of them

explanation.surface: Someone exploits their place living quietly inside a public body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silent' looks like it describes the institution; it gives MUM, as in 'keep mum'.
explanation.definitionFit: A building holding collections open to visitors, usually state funded, is a classic public establishment.

clue.text: Name given to threads in fabrics

indicators.note: given to here means handed into, so one piece is put inside another

blocks.note: lines are threads or cords
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A name is assigned to the yarns used in cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like naming types of yarn; 'Name' is simply N, slipped into the threads.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloths woven from flax are a family of textiles, so the plural noun matches the plural definition.

clue.text: Lady in Burgundy produced white wine containing iodine

indicators.note: to contain something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: made means produced
Moselle is a German white wine from the Moselle valley
I is the chemical symbol for iodine

explanation.surface: A woman in Burgundy makes a white wine with iodine in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Burgundy also suggests red wine, steering towards wine-making; here it just places the lady in France.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the French title for an unmarried young woman, so it is what a lady in a French region would be called.

clue.text: Second unfinished drink

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its end, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: of two things mentioned, the second one is the later-named one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a moment of time, but it means the latter of two.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso with lots of steamed milk is a popular coffee drink served in cafés.

clue.text: Drive somewhat begrudgingly northbound

indicators.note: 'somewhat' means to some degree, so only a portion of the text is used
in a down clue heading north means travelling upwards, so the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: letters two to five of the word

explanation.surface: Someone drives north with a bit of reluctance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' sounds like motoring with 'northbound'; it is the noun meaning an impulse.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong inner impulse or desire can be called a drive, as in sex drive, which is what this noun means.

clue.text: Student welcoming drops in support on course

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a tee is the peg supporting a golf ball on the course
raindrops; rain falls in drops

explanation.surface: A student taking a course is offered help, which is welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On course' suggests studying; it is a golf course, where a tee holds up the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone learning a job or skill under instruction is a learner, so the noun matches a student.

clue.text: Club failing to open, say

indicators.note: failing to open means missing the start, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: a putter is a golf club

explanation.surface: A nightclub that never managed to open its doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' suggests a nightclub that fails to open; it is a golf club, losing its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak or voice words aloud is to say them, so this verb is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Unsigned band’s music made money, to some extent

indicators.note: 'to some extent' means partly, so only a portion of the text is used

blocks.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: An unsigned band's music earned some money, after a fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the long phrase at the front; the answer runs across the gap between two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Bands without a record deal send labels a rough recording to show what they can do, which is exactly this word.

clue.text: Sort of sweater I knotted

indicators.note: knotted means tangled up, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone describes the kind of jumper they knitted themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' looks like it introduces a kind of sweater, but it is the definition, a hedging phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases hedge a statement, admitting the wording is approximate or figurative, so they are interchangeable idioms.
